clue.text: Discover the meaning of fish in a river

indicators.note: the fish is placed in the river, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
a cod is a fish

explanation.surface: Instructions for a naturalist working out what a fish found in a river means.
explanation.definitionFit: To work out the sense of a coded message or puzzling sign is to crack it.

clue.text: In time Reds could develop faults

indicators.note: the letters may develop into another arrangement

explanation.surface: Communists given time might show their flaws.
explanation.definitionFit: Black marks or shortcomings counted against someone.

clue.text: Surely no-one could have had a poor opinion of him?

definitions.text: Surely no-one could have had a poor opinion of him?

parts.words: Surely no-one could have had a poor opinion of him?
parts.note: 'poor' can mean low or thinking him penniless; this king was proverbially wealthy

explanation.surface: Someone so admired that nobody could think badly of him.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'poor opinion' as disapproval; the trick is that nobody could think him poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lydian king famous for vast riches, a byword for wealth.

clue.text: Hurry to the directors in a car

definitions.note: the clue names where the item is, rather than the item

parts.note: to dash is to hurry
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: Rushing to a board meeting by car.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument panel facing a driver, found in every motor vehicle.

clue.text: Under which a Welsh poet wrote

definitions.text: Under which a Welsh poet wrote

parts.words: Under which a Welsh poet wrote
parts.note: reads as a poet writing beneath trees, but points to the title of Dylan Thomas's radio play, whose first word is 'Under'

explanation.surface: A Welsh bard composing in the shade of some trees.
explanation.walkthrough: Dylan Thomas's play for voices is 'Under Milk Wood'; the clue supplies 'Under' and asks for the rest of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas set his famous radio play in a fictional Welsh village beneath this named wood.

clue.text: Tales of the frozen North?

parts.note: stories from the cold northern island nation, whose name suggests ice

explanation.surface: Stories of Arctic adventure.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval prose narratives from the Norse settlement of Iceland, about families and heroes.

clue.text: What skinheads go to football matches for?

definitions.text: What skinheads go to football matches for?

parts.words: What skinheads go to football matches for?
parts.note: thrills, and also the booting that football and fighting both involve

explanation.surface: Asking why hooligans turn up at games.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both thrills and blows with the foot, so the thugs go for excitement and for violence.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for thrills or excitement, and also blows struck with the foot.

clue.text: One of those pieces of eight

definitions.text: One of those pieces of eight

parts.words: One of those pieces of eight
parts.note: not the pirate's Spanish coin but a piece of music for eight players

explanation.surface: A pirate's coin from the treasure chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces of eight' suggests Spanish silver dollars; here it is a musical composition for eight performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical work scored for eight instruments or voices.

clue.text: Copper is accompanying a girl- consternation!

parts.note: d was the abbreviation for the old British copper penny
taken as written
May is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A policeman walking out with a young woman causes alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the old penny, abbreviated d in pre-decimal British money.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay is alarm and distress at something unexpected, a synonym of shocked concern.

clue.text: Like the saint who has taken the vow of poverty?

definitions.text: Like the saint who has taken the vow of poverty?

parts.words: Like the saint who has taken the vow of poverty?
parts.note: the saint is good, and having vowed poverty he has nothing, so '...'

explanation.surface: Describing a holy man sworn to poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means worthless, but read literally it describes someone good who owns nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Worthless or useless, the usual sense of the phrase, here split into virtuous and possessionless.

clue.text: Novel subject of a 1969's sensational scoop

explanation.surface: A book about the big story of 1969.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1969 the Apollo astronauts scooped up rock from the lunar surface, the sensational 'scoop' of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins wrote a famous Victorian detective story of that title; also lunar rock collected by Apollo 11 in 1969.

clue.text: Delicacies with which an old conspirator got by

indicators.note: the conspirator's full name is only got once by is attached, so taking those letters away leaves the word wanted

parts.note: Robert Catesby led the Gunpowder Plot of 1605
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old plotter survived on fine food.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Catesby was the ringleader of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot; add BY to the answer and you get his name, so with it he 'got BY'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cates is an archaic word for choice foods or dainties.

clue.text: "A set with little wilful thorns " (Tennyson)

parts.note: a quotation with a word missing after 'A', to be filled from Tennyson's poem Maud

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a blank after 'A': Tennyson's Maud has 'A rosebud set with little wilful thorns'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorny stems carry flower buds, and Tennyson's line describes a young bloom guarded by prickles.

clue.text: Took the chair inter alia in Whitefriars

indicators.note: Latin for among or between, so the sitting goes in among the letters of alia

parts.note: taken as written, the Latin word from the phrase
to take a chair is to sit, so this gives sat

explanation.surface: Someone presided, among other things, in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inter alia' looks like one Latin phrase, but 'inter' is the container signal and 'alia' the word that is split open. Alsatia was the old cant name for Whitefriars, a lawless sanctuary area of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Whitefriars precinct of London, a refuge for debtors and criminals, was nicknamed by this cant name in the 17th century.

clue.text: Singing part for a Scot, perhaps

indicators.note: signals that the letters given are only one possible arrangement, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A role written for a Scottish singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's opera heroine is a title role for a soprano.

clue.text: Grandfather clock ?

parts.note: an elderly man is a grandfather, and a clock is a timer, so an aged person read literally as an aged timepiece

explanation.surface: A tall clock in the hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran or elderly person, one who has been around a long time, like a grandfather.

clue.text: Stimulus to tin production in Venice perhaps

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a new product, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Something to encourage tin manufacture in Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: A motivation or spur that encourages action.

clue.text: Condition of one with no calling?

definitions.text: Condition of one with no calling?

parts.words: Condition of one with no calling?
parts.note: calling suggests a vocation, but here it is what one is called

explanation.surface: The state of someone without a vocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like a career; read as what one is called, it is someone with no name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anonymous, without a name by which one is known.

clue.text: Scorn aid with such a twisted smile

definitions.text: Scorn aid with such a twisted smile

indicators.note: the letters of scorn aid are bent out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sneering at help with a crooked grin.
explanation.definitionFit: A mocking, scornful smile is described as cynical or derisive, the kind of sneer that scorns help.

clue.text: Cut down a river 'crossing

parts.note: a bridge is a way across a river

explanation.surface: A river crossing being demolished.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten a text by trimming parts out is to condense it.

clue.text: In Rome was he as bad a poet as he sounded?

definitions.text: In Rome was he as bad a poet as he sounded?

parts.words: In Rome was he as bad a poet as he sounded?
parts.note: refers to the Roman poet in Julius Caesar who is killed for his bad verses, and whose name is said like 'sinner'

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a Roman poet was as wicked as his name.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar the mob tears apart Cinna the poet 'for his bad verses'; his name is pronounced like 'sinner'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Roman poet in Julius Caesar is mistaken for a conspirator and killed by a crowd.

clue.text: Hurried back at some speed to tell the tale

indicators.note: the word for hurried is turned back to front

parts.note: ran means hurried
a rate is a speed

explanation.surface: Someone racing home quickly to tell their story.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story or give an account of events.

clue.text: It served to keep war-time charges down

definitions.text: It served to keep war-time charges down

parts.words: It served to keep war-time charges down
parts.note: charges are the gunpowder loads in an old muzzle-loading gun, pushed down by a rod

explanation.surface: Something that held down wartime prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' and 'down' suggest wartime price controls; it is the rod for packing powder and shot into a musket.
explanation.definitionFit: The rod used to push powder and ball down the barrel of a muzzle-loading firearm.

clue.text: Most of the month, bed means fruit.

indicators.note: all but the final letter of the month is used

parts.note: April is a month
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Spending much of a month in bed eating fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A small orange stone fruit related to the peach.

clue.text: Sarah Battle took them in hand

definitions.text: Sarah Battle took them in hand

parts.words: Sarah Battle took them in hand
parts.note: Charles Lamb's essay on Mrs Sarah Battle tells of her love of whist, played with a hand of these

explanation.surface: A formidable lady taking charge of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Battle is the whist-loving old lady of Charles Lamb's essay 'Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing pieces held in a hand at whist and other games.

clue.text: A Scot's own genealogy, of course

parts.note: ain is the Scots word for own
a family tree records genealogy

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's family history, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but 'course' is the definition. Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse of the Grand National.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse near Liverpool that hosts the Grand National steeplechase.

clue.text: Not an original clause, but one that is carried

explanation.surface: Distinguishing an added clause from something carried.
explanation.definitionFit: An amendment added to a bill or contract, not part of its first draft; also a horseman, borne by his mount.

clue.text: I'm in a neat condition, albeit lifeless

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new condition or state, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tidy but lacking all energy.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone or a table is without life, not alive.

clue.text: Not Lady Godiva's equestrian display, one would think

definitions.text: Not Lady Godiva's equestrian display, one would think

parts.words: Not Lady Godiva's equestrian display, one would think
parts.note: Lady Godiva rode naked, so her ride lacked clothing; the horse-show event's name seems to begin with clothing

explanation.surface: Lady Godiva's famous ride through Coventry was no show-ring event.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Godiva legendarily rode naked through Coventry; the answer looks as if it involves dress, which she lacked.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitive horse-riding discipline in which the horse performs precise trained movements.

clue.text: The poetry of France can be uplifting

definitions.note: a noun is wanted; here the clue means things that can lift

parts.note: le is French for the
vers is French for verse or poetry

explanation.surface: French poetry can be inspiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifting' suggests inspiration, but the answer is the plural noun: bars used to prise loads up.
explanation.definitionFit: Bars pivoting on a fulcrum are used to raise heavy weights.
